title: Affordable Broadband and Global Economic Convergence
subtitle: The augmented Solow-Swan framework, open-access wholesale infrastructure, spectrum economics, and the century convergence dividend
description: A century-scale framework (2000–2100) arguing that affordable broadband is a general-purpose technology for economic convergence and that four pillars (open-access wholesale networks, spectrum abundance, digital public rails and human capital) can deliver it, in twelve chapters from growth theory and tariffs to spectrum, trade, finance, subsidies and case studies.
contribution: A twelve-chapter monograph on affordable broadband and economic convergence: an augmented growth model, bandwidth poverty and tariffs, telecom market structure and open-access networks, spectrum policy, digital trade, finance, human capital, regional corridors, public-sector productivity and subsidy design, with a four-pillar framework and a lexicon of its own terms.
abstract: Affordable, high-speed broadband is presented as a general-purpose technology that shifts the national production frontier and drives economic convergence between poorer and richer countries. The monograph argues that low-income economies stay in low-productivity traps because of market friction and information asymmetries, that high broadband prices, device import duties and concentrated telecom markets impose a regressive penalty on poor users, and that competition, open-access wholesale infrastructure and better spectrum policy can lower prices and expand use.

It proposes four pillars: open-access wholesale infrastructure, spectrum abundance with coverage obligations, interoperable digital public rails, and human capital and cognitive arbitrage through cloud compute and AI. The monograph is organised in twelve chapters covering an augmented growth model, bandwidth poverty, telecom industrial organization, spectrum economics, digital trade, financial rails, human capital, regional corridors, public-sector productivity, subsidy architecture and case studies, and closes with a century-scale synthesis across four planning periods from 2000 to 2100. It includes a lexicon of the framework’s defined terms.
coreProposition: Affordable, high-speed broadband functions as a general-purpose technology that shifts the national production possibility frontier, acting as a primary catalyst for macroeconomic convergence.

keyFindings.title: Convergence has not been automatic.
keyFindings.text: The monograph argues that low-income countries have repeatedly become trapped in low-productivity equilibria, caused by spatial market friction, geographic isolation and information asymmetries, and that broadband can help them escape.

keyFindings.title: A regressive bandwidth penalty.
keyFindings.text: It argues that low-income users buying small prepaid data passes pay far more per gigabyte than affluent subscribers, and that entry-level broadband costs far more than the UN’s 2%-of-income affordability benchmark, compounded by import duties on smartphones.

keyFindings.title: Competition and open access.
keyFindings.text: It proposes antitrust action against concentrated telecom markets, local loop unbundling, and carrier-neutral wholesale open-access networks.

keyFindings.title: Spectrum and exchange points.
keyFindings.text: It proposes replacing revenue-maximizing spectrum auctions with coverage-obligation licensing and dynamic spectrum sharing, and carrier-neutral regional internet exchange points to stop local traffic being routed abroad.

keyFindings.title: Trade, finance and human capital.
keyFindings.text: It proposes digital trade rails, open payment switches and digital public infrastructure, and cloud compute and AI to let knowledge workers in developing countries sell services globally.

keyFindings.title: Subsidies, cases and a century in four periods.
keyFindings.text: It proposes least-cost reverse subsidy auctions, device financing and vouchers, draws on Vietnam, India, Costa Rica and Rwanda, and sets out a strategy through infrastructure awakening (2000–2025), universal affordability (2025–2050), autonomous integration (2050–2075) and planetary knowledge parity (2075–2100).

glossary.definition: The measure of aggregate economic output efficiency gains that cannot be accounted for by simple capital or labor inputs, said to be accelerated by general-purpose digital technologies.
The market distortion whereby low-income users purchasing micro-metered prepaid daily data passes pay unit rates up to 80 times higher per gigabyte than affluent postpaid subscribers.
The proposed inflection point in population penetration at which broadband network externalities ignite self-reinforcing enterprise formation and economic growth.
A standard antitrust metric of market concentration; values above 2,500 denote concentrated markets, while developing telecom duopolies are stated to routinely exceed 4,500.
A regulatory mandate requiring incumbent network owners to lease dark fiber and conduit ducts to competing retail service providers at cost-oriented, non-discriminatory rates.
A carrier-neutral, utility-scale physical infrastructure entity legally restricted to wholesale bandwidth sales, preventing anti-competitive self-preferencing.
An administrative allocation framework awarding prime spectrum at nominal cost in exchange for legally binding commitments to achieve 95% or more rural broadband coverage.
An automated, cognitive frequency management regime allowing secondary users to transmit across temporarily unoccupied licensed radio bands without interference.
High-value professional, scientific, administrative, and creative services that can be transmitted across cross-border fiber rails without moving physical freight.
The foundational triad of open, interoperable digital rails (biometric identity, real-time payment switches, and verifiable data registries) operating as public goods.
The phenomenon where high-skill knowledge workers in developing economies earn global remote wages over broadband while residing domestically, recycling wealth locally.
A routing failure where intra-regional data traverses intercontinental subsea cables to overseas hubs before returning, multiplying latency and foreign-exchange costs.
A physical facility where competing ISPs, content networks, and mobile operators interconnect to exchange local traffic without paying international transit fees.
A competitive procurement model where operators bid for the lowest one-time government grant required to build open-access broadband in unserved rural zones.
An asset-backed micro-leasing model that allows low-income users to acquire smartphones for $5 down and daily $0.30 mobile money payments with remote locking.
The cumulative century-scale macroeconomic expansion (stated as $42 trillion or more by 2100) said to be realized when universal, affordable broadband closes the global productivity divide.
